title: General liability risk assessment with AI: a score you cannot decompose is one you cannot defend
summary: In general liability risk assessment, AI should assemble and verify the evidence, so every score traces to its source and holds up with reinsurers.
body_markdown:
The return on AI in general liability risk assessment is decided at risk selection, because in a line where severity keeps compounding, the account you decline matters far more than the hour you save on data entry. The useful question for a carrier is whether a general liability risk score holds up when a claim, a reinsurer or a regulator asks the underwriter to defend it, since almost any model can produce a number. A score that cannot be decomposed into its parts cannot be defended, and in a market shaped by nuclear verdicts an indefensible score usually means a loss that was priced in without anyone noticing. This changes what we should expect from AI in the first place. Its job is to make the risk evidence complete and verifiable, while the underwriter continues to own the judgment and the machine owns the assembly, the extraction and the audit trail behind each field. Carriers that reverse this order tend to automate their way into faster adverse selection, which is the opposite of what they bought the tool to do.


## What is AI-assisted general liability risk assessment?


AI-assisted general liability risk assessment is the use of AI to assemble, extract and verify the data that a GL risk score depends on, so the underwriter can score the risk from clean, sourced information. The AI reads the[loss runs](https://pibit.ai/insurance-knowledge/loss-run) , applications and supplementals, and it structures the claims history, classification and exposure basis, while expert validation is brought into the picture for the fields where the model's confidence is low. The risk judgment stays with the underwriter, and what the AI takes away is the manual data work that tends to delay and distort that judgment.


This matters because general liability submissions are heavy with evidence. A single account can carry years of loss runs, several supplementals and class codes that conflict with each other, and when that data is keyed in by hand the errors and gaps come in with it, so the score inherits every one of them. Pibit AI treats the application document as the ground truth and links each extracted field back to its source through[extraction and research](https://pibit.ai/extraction-and-research) , which means the score rests on evidence the underwriter can open and inspect.


## Why is risk selection the margin lever in general liability right now?


Risk selection is the margin lever today because casualty severity is rising faster than rate can keep up with it, and general liability is firming on[social inflation](https://pibit.ai/insurance-knowledge/social-inflation) far more than on frequency. According to the Swiss Re Institute, US liability claims rose 57% over the prior decade, and social inflation added roughly 7% a year to liability claim costs in 2024, the highest rate in two decades.[Nuclear verdicts](https://pibit.ai/insurance-knowledge/nuclear-verdicts) also cluster by venue and plaintiff profile, so two accounts that look alike on paper can carry very different tail risk.


Commercial auto shows where this ends when selection lags behind severity. As per AM Best (September 2025), the line posted a $4.9B underwriting loss in 2024 at a 107.2 combined ratio, its 14th consecutive losing year, and rate increases alone did not fix it.


Commercial auto combined ratio in 2024 was 107.2 against a 100 break-even line, a $4.9B underwriting loss in its 14th straight losing year (AM Best, September 2025).


When severity compounds, the loss ratio is won or lost at the point of selection, and selection can only be as good as the claims and exposure data behind it. A carrier that reads the loss history faster without reading it more accurately will simply decline and bind the wrong accounts sooner. We go deeper on this in[the real cost of inaccurate underwriting data](https://pibit.ai/blog/real-cost-inaccurate-underwriting-data-commercial-p-c) and in[how data accuracy drives the commercial auto loss ratio](https://pibit.ai/blog/commercial-auto-underwriting-data-accuracy-loss-ratio) .


## What data decides a general liability risk score?


Five inputs move a GL score, each of them sits inside unstructured documents, and the score is only as reliable as the weakest of the five.


Risk input Where it hides Why it moves premium


Loss history Loss runs, prior-carrier claims data Sets the expected burn rate and reserve adequacy for the account


Classification and exposure basis ACORD applications, supplementals, class codes A wrong class or payroll base misprices the entire account


Prior litigation and venue Claim narratives, jurisdiction of past suits Nuclear-verdict exposure concentrates by venue and plaintiff profile


Contractual risk transfer Certificates, additional-insured and indemnity terms Caps or expands the carrier's net retained exposure


Operations and hazard detail Supplementals, site and operations descriptions Drives the frequency assumption behind the base rate


None of these fields is optional, because a missed venue pattern underprices tail risk and a missed class code misprices the base, which makes extraction accuracy a risk-selection issue in its own right. Our[accuracy benchmark for AI underwriting](https://pibit.ai/blog/ai-underwriting-accuracy-benchmark-99-percent) explains why a 95% field-level rate falls short of production for casualty work, and the[risk scoring](https://pibit.ai/insurance-knowledge/risk-scoring) entry in our glossary covers how the inputs combine.


## Should AI score the risk, or assemble the evidence?


AI should assemble and verify the evidence and leave the verdict to the underwriter, since this is the line most tools blur and the place where underwriters lose trust in them. A frequent objection in casualty teams is that AI makes too many inferences about risk that underwriters should decide for themselves. That objection is fair, and the fix sits in the architecture. Pibit AI scores each risk factor deterministically through[triage and risk analysis](https://pibit.ai/triaging-and-risk-analysis) , and each factor, 80 or more for some lines, is visible, scored on its own and tied to the data behind it.


The accuracy that makes this safe comes from a managed pipeline around the model. Pibit AI pairs AI extraction with expert validation and guarantees 99.9% field-level accuracy with our human-in-the-loop, in the contract, so low-confidence fields route to a reviewer before they ever reach the score. The output is evidence an underwriter can act on, which saves them from double-checking a guess.


The payoff is capacity that moves toward judgment. Once the data work is handled, senior underwriters can spend their hours on the accounts where venue, contracts and loss patterns really need interpretation, which is how carriers grow premium without growing headcount, a point we develop in our guide to[underwriter capacity in a soft market](https://pibit.ai/blog/underwriter-capacity-commercial-pc-grow-gwp-2026-soft-market) .


## How do you make a general liability risk score defensible?


A general liability risk score is defensible when every signal in it can be traced back to its source document, so decomposability is the practical test. If an underwriter cannot see which factors raised or lowered the score, a reinsurer, an auditor or a court will not be able to see it either. The NAIC AI governance framework, approved in late 2025, pushes carriers toward this kind of oversight, testing and transparency for AI-assisted decisions, and a single aggregate score with no lineage fails that standard straight away.


Field-level provenance is what turns a score into a record. Every extracted value should carry a link to the page and field it came from, and every human correction should be logged, because that audit trail is what lets a carrier defend a declination or a price twice: once to the reinsurer who shares the tail, and once to the regulator who reviews the model. We cover the standard in[field-level provenance as the AI underwriting audit standard](https://pibit.ai/blog/field-level-provenance-ai-underwriting-audit-standard) . In a market shaped by nuclear verdicts, the carrier that can show its work holds an edge that a faster black box cannot give it.


## How should carriers evaluate AI for general liability risk assessment?


Carriers should judge the tool on whether it produces a defensible score, since speed is easy to demo and expensive to trust on its own.


Criterion What good looks like What should worry you


Field-level accuracy A contractual SLA on every extracted field Best-effort accuracy or sampled QA only


Scoring transparency Deterministic, factor-level, every signal visible One aggregate score from a black-box model


Expert validation In-house review on low-confidence fields Fully automated output with no review step


Evidence trail Every field linked to its source document A score with no provenance or lineage


System fit An API layer on the existing policy system A full migration or rip-and-replace


Exception handling Edge cases route to a senior underwriter Thin-data accounts forced to an auto-decision


The most useful evaluation runs on your own declined and bound accounts, with a vendor demo set as a distant second. You can ask any tool to reproduce last year's hardest general liability files and show the evidence behind each score, and the right system will make the underwriter faster and more defensible at the same time, while the wrong one only speeds the path to the same bad risk.


General liability rewards the carrier that selects well, and selection is a data problem before it becomes a judgment problem. AI earns its place when it hands the underwriter complete, sourced and decomposable evidence and leaves the call with them, which is what separates a score that wins the account from a score that cannot survive the claim.
